papers.title: Evaluating the Evaluation of Music Generation Models with Generative Psychometrics
papers.abstract: Subjective user studies are one of the major methods for evaluating music generation models. However, subjective evaluation protocols vary widely and are rarely specified in enough detail to be reproduced, hindering comparison across studies. In this paper, we map subjective evaluation methods in ISMIR music generation papers from 2020-2025 and apply generative psychometrics to assess the stability of their items. We extract 284 items from the papers' methodological descriptions, using an LLM and manual validation to standardize them. We represent these items as contextual embeddings and apply Unique Variable Analysis to remove redundant, locally dependent items and Bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis to estimate their latent dimensions. Results show the network converges onto a taxonomy of six stable quality dimensions: Rhythm, Melody, Audio, Composition, Structure, and Lyrics, pointing to a unified methodology for conducting user studies to evaluate music generation models.
papers.venue: Accepted to the 2nd Latin American Music Information Retrieval (LAMIR) workshop

papers.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPLICATIONS FOR IMPROVING PRONUNCIATION SKILLS OF AUTISTIC PATIENTS: A CRITICAL REVIEW
papers.abstract: Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) is a developmental disorder and individuals with ASD experience challenges in social relation, communication, as well as speech articulation. Many children with ASD have significant difficulty pronouncing words properly, presenting difficulties with learning at school and communicating in day-to-day situations. Recently, AI has demonstrated high potential and application value in many therapeutic and educational applications, speech and pronunciation training among others. AI systems typically integrate speech recognition, text-to-speech synthesis, automatic feedback and interactive learning environments. However, even with this progress, the existing solutions still have limitations such as limited vocabulary, lack of real-time interaction and poor adaptation to different dialects and cultural backgrounds. In this paper, a review of AI techniques that have been proposed to enhance pronunciation skills in children with ASD is offered. The review included 44 peer-reviewed articles obtained from Scopus database. We indicate current research trends, reflect existing gaps, and propose directions toward the development of more adaptive, inclusive, and cultural responsive AI-pedestal pronunciation training tools for improving communication skills and quality of life in children with ASD

papers.title: High-Fidelity Binarized Neural Vocoder
papers.abstract: Neural vocoders have achieved remarkable progress in high-fidelity waveform generation in recent years, but most existing methods still rely on full-precision operators, leading to non-negligible storage and computational costs during inference. Binary neural networks (BNNs) provide an alternative direction by quantizing weights and activations to 1 bit. However, directly applying binarization to neural vocoders is rather challenging as it inherently incurs severe information loss. To this end, we propose BiVoC, a BNN-oriented time-frequency neural vocoder for high-fidelity waveform generation. Building on our previous full-precision RNDVoC framework, BiVoC adapts the inverse-problem formulation, range-null decomposition, and fineto-coarse non-uniform subband modeling to the 1-bit setting. Specifically, we develop a simple binarized convolutional unit to provide stable time-frequency feature modeling under binary representations. Furthermore, we analyze the quality-complexity sensitivity of different modules and propose a mixed-precision design to retain quality-sensitive components in full precision while binarizing computation-dominant parts. Extensive experiments are conducted on LibriTTS and multiple out-of-distribution benchmarks. Both objective and subjective results demonstrate that BiVoC substantially outperforms BNN variants obtained by directly binarizing existing vocoders, while achieving competitive performance against several mainstream full-precision vocoder baselines under much lower theoretical computational cost. These results demonstrate the promising potential of BNNs in the audio generation field. Codes and pre-trained weights are available at https://github.com/Andong-Li-speech/BiVoC.
papers.venue: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing 2026, 15 pages, 10 figures, 16 tables

papers.title: Beyond Co-Generation: Rethinking Jointness in Joint Audio-Video Generation
papers.abstract: Our aim is to advance the understanding of genuine audio-visual coordination in joint text-to-audio-video (T2AV) generation, with particular emphasis on semantic consistency. Evaluating audio-visual consistency in T2AV generation is nontrivial, as detailed text prompts obscure whether such consistency stems from genuine cross-modal coordination or merely from independent text following. To isolate the former, we introduce intrinsic jointness: the ability of audio and video to produce the same realization for details left underspecified by the prompt. Using semantically underspecified prompts (e.g., "musical instrument playing" rather than "electric guitar playing"), we investigate four recent models and reveal their limited intrinsic jointness. To address this limitation, we propose JointREPA, a simple representation alignment-based post-training method to facilitate cross-modal coordination. Since existing benchmarks use semantically detailed prompts, we introduce UNSAIDBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate intrinsic jointness under semantic underspecification. Experiments across two distinct models and three benchmarks, including UNSAIDBench, demonstrate that JointREPA consistently improves semantic consistency.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash

Hear clearly. Understand deeply. Act intelligently.

Ming-3.0-audio-flash is a native audio-language model from inclusionAI. It accepts audio together with text instructions and supports speech recognition, spoken question answering, audio understanding, audio reasoning, and optional synthesized-speech responses.
GitHub · 🤖 ModelScope · 🤗 Flash · 🤗 Tiny · 💻 Examples
## Model Summary | Property | Description | | --- | --- | | Developer | inclusionAI | | Model type | Native audio-language Mixture-of-Experts model | | Parameters | 126B total parameters, 6.5B activated per inference step | | Inputs | Audio and text instructions | | Outputs | Text, or text with optional synthesized speech | | Primary languages | Chinese and English, including varied accents and dialects | | License | MIT | ## Highlights - **Complex speech recognition:** Handles Chinese and English speech, dialects, accents, noisy environments, and multi-speaker recordings. - **Long-audio understanding:** Comprehends and analyzes long-form recordings. - **Multidimensional perception:** Understands speech, non-speech sounds, acoustic scenes, and music. - **Audio reasoning:** Answers questions and performs reasoning over audio content. - **Audio interaction:** Produces text responses and can optionally synthesize speech with built-in voices or a reference voice. ## Architecture Ming-3.0-audio-flash combines an audio encoder and projector with a Mixture-of-Experts language backbone. An optional Talker generates speech responses from the model's output.

## Quick Start with Transformers The model uses custom Transformers code. Review the repository code before enabling `trust_remote_code=True`. ```bash git clone https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash.git cd Ming-3.0-audio-flash python -m venv .venv-transformers source .venv-transformers/bin/activate pip install -r requirements-transformers.txt ``` ### Audio Understanding ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --prompt "Please answer the question in the audio." ``` ### Speech Recognition ```bash python examples/transformers_audio.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --task asr \ --max-new-tokens 256 \ --no-repeat-ngram-size 10 ``` The validated ASR prompt asks the model to identify the spoken language and place a tab between the language label and transcription. ### Direct Python Usage ```python import torch from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash" audio_path = "examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained( model_id, trust_remote_code=True, use_fast=False, ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto", trust_remote_code=True, ).eval() messages = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "audio", "audio": audio_path}, {"type": "text", "text": "Please answer the question in the audio."}, ], } ] inputs = processor(messages).to(model.device) inputs["audio_feats"] = inputs["audio_feats"].to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens=512, do_sample=False, ) generated_ids = output_ids[0, inputs["input_ids"].shape[1] :] response = processor.decode(generated_ids, skip_special_tokens=True).strip() print(response) ``` ## Speech Output The Talker example supports built-in voices and reference-audio voice prompting: ```bash python examples/transformers_thinker_talker.py \ --model inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --audio examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --voice US_Stella \ --output output.wav ``` See the [voice guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/docs/voices.md) for available voice names and reference-audio usage. ## Serving ### vLLM-Omni ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=text ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The reference 128K serving profile uses tensor parallelism across four 80 GB H800 GPUs. Select the deployment YAML that matches text-only or Talker output. On particularly long audio inputs, the four-GPU profiles may OOM; in that case, switch to the corresponding eight-GPU fallback profile (`deploy/*_8gpu.yaml`), which sets `tensor_parallel_size: 8` across GPUs 0–7 (and the Talker reuses GPU 7). See the [deployment guide](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/README.md#vllm-omni) for details. For speech output, start the audio profile and select an IP or registered voice with the vLLM-Omni client's `--voice` option: ```bash MING_OUTPUT_MODE=audio ./scripts/serve_vllm_omni.sh "$MODEL_PATH" python examples/vllm_omni_audio_chat.py examples/audio/introduce_ant_group.wav \ --audio-response \ --voice US_Stella \ --output-audio outputs/answer.wav ``` The client sends this selection as Chat Completions `audio.voice: {"id": "..."}`. vLLM-Omni uses the built-in IP voice `灵小柔` when no voice is specified. The model directory also provides `灵楷` and `US_James` as preset reference voices under `voice_presets/voice_audio/`, with their matching transcripts in `voice_presets/voice_prompts.json`. Both names are also available as built-in IP voices. ### SGLang ```bash export MODEL_PATH=inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash ./scripts/serve_sglang.sh "$MODEL_PATH" ``` The validated SGLang profile uses four GPUs and provides text output. See the [SGLang example](https://github.com/inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash/blob/main/examples/sglang_audio_chat.py) for client usage. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/) serves transcription, audio chat, and speech synthesis from one server. Serving uses two GPUs: `--thinker.tp_size 2` places the thinker on both visible devices, the audio encoder uses GPU 0, and speech synthesis uses GPU 1. ```bash CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 sgl-omni serve \ --model-path inclusionAI/Ming-3.0-audio-flash \ --thinker.tp_size 2 ``` The server exposes OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, `/v1/audio/speech`, and `/v1/chat/completions` endpoints. See the [SGLang-Omni cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/ming3_audio.html) for client examples, including voice cloning with `ref_audio` and `ref_text`. ## Evaluation ### Speech Reasoning (Big Bench Audio) Ming-3.0-audio-flash achieves **99.8%** on Artificial Analysis's Big Bench Audio benchmark, ranking **#1 overall among all closed-source and open-source models** on the leaderboard shown below.

# Model Overview ### Description NVIDIA Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe is an offline speech and audio model that processes recordings, together with text instructions and optional context, into text responses. The audio understanding mixture and the pretrained base components may also contain web-derived data. ### Internally Generated Data, Including Prompt-Collected Data NVIDIA-generated or NVIDIA-transformed training artifacts include: - Granary v2 pseudo-transcriptions and model-generated translations, together with human-improved and Riva-labeled variants - Prompt-controlled Granary v2 task expansions for transcription, contextual transcription, speech QA, inverse text normalization, disfluency-reduced transcription, captioning, and code-switched transcription - Fine-, coarse-, distractor-, partial-, and negative-context variants for contextual ASR - Long-form transcription data and transcript-plus-QA, timestamp, speaker-tag, and translation variants - Multi-speaker task formatting and constructed audio mixtures - Non-speech vocalization and speaking-style annotations - Balanced language-identification prompts and targets - PII tagging and redaction examples - No-speech abstention prompts and empty-response targets - Curated Nemotron text SFT data, audio-instruction, audio-reasoning, and safety-tuning blends Training prompts are developer-authored or generated task instructions associated with prepared training examples. User interactions with a deployed product or model were not used to train the model. ### Self-Sourced Synthetic Data Synthetic and model-generated training data include: - **Nemotron-PII text data:** fully synthetic text examples covering more than 55 PII/PHI categories, with tagged and redacted outputs - **PII-aware ASR data:** synthetic multilingual PII-positive speech examples - **Constructed multi-speaker mixtures:** AuMix examples combining source recordings into conversations of up to eight speakers, including long-form mixtures - **Granary v2 task variants:** generated contextual terms and distractors, speech questions and answers, captions, code-switched targets, and transcript-plus-QA/translation variants - **Audio understanding synthetic-data-generation subsets:** generated captions, questions, answers, instruction-following targets, and reasoning traces for sound, music, speech, and audio-reasoning tasks - **Prompt augmentation:** deterministic and generated prompt variants for transcription, language identification, PII handling, and no-speech abstention Pseudo-labeled ASR and translation examples retain source audio and use model-generated labels; they should not be described as synthetic audio. Constructed multi-speaker mixtures likewise combine source recordings rather than generating new speaker identities. ### Testing Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Labeling Method by dataset:** Not Applicable **Properties:** Not Applicable - Testing uses the public benchmark test sets described under [Evaluation Dataset](#evaluation-dataset); there is no separate held-out testing dataset. ### Evaluation Dataset **Data Collection Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Collected, Automated **Labeling Method by dataset:** Hybrid: Manually-Labeled, Automatic/Sensors **Properties:** - **Data count:** more than 330,000 test examples from public benchmarks, including approximately 243,000 for English, multilingual, multi-speaker, and contextual transcription; 29,000 for language identification; and 57,000 for audio understanding, voice instruction following, and text-only reasoning. Speech translation, long-form, code-switched, and entity benchmarks are evaluated in addition. - **Modalities:** audio with text instructions, references, and context; text-only for the text reasoning benchmarks. - **Nature of the content:** read speech (LibriSpeech, Multilingual LibriSpeech, FLEURS, Common Voice), parliamentary speech (VoxPopuli), podcasts and online video (GigaSpeech), financial earnings calls (Earnings-22, SPGISpeech), meetings (AMI, NOTSOFAR-1, AISHELL-4, AliMeeting), telephone conversations (CALLHOME), interviews (Mixer 6), noisy and degraded recordings (URGENT 2024), code-switched conversations, spoken questions and instructions (VoiceBench, Spoken-MQA), and speech, sound, and music for audio understanding (MMAU, MMAR, AIR-Bench). - **Linguistic characteristics:** 40 supported languages, with the largest share in English, including Indian-accented English and Hindi (Monsoon), Mandarin meetings, and Hindi–English, Bengali–English, and Mandarin–English code-switching; transcripts are scored both verbatim and in normalized written form, depending on the benchmark. ### Benchmark Results Results are grouped by task. **↓ Lower is better; ↑ higher is better.** Error rates and accuracy are percentages unless another scale is shown. Install both into one environment with [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) and download the checkpoint: ```bash git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech.git nemo-speech cd nemo-speech uv venv --python 3.13 .venv UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=$PWD/.venv uv sync --extra asr --extra vllm --locked --no-install-project uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps -e . # PyAV decodes compressed audio formats, such as M4A, without a system FFmpeg. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps av==19.0.2 # vLLM requires OpenCV, which NeMo's dependency settings exclude. uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python --no-deps opencv-python-headless==5.0.0.93 source .venv/bin/activate hf download nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B --local-dir ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B ``` #### Start the Server Start an OpenAI-compatible server on one GPU, with MTP speculative decoding proposing eight tokens (MTP8): ```bash export VLLM_PLUGINS=nemo_speechlm # Allow vLLM to decode recordings up to one hour long (the default is 600 seconds). export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_DECODE_DURATION_S=3600 export VLLM_MAX_AUDIO_CLIP_FILESIZE_MB=180 # Word timestamps require the V1 model runner. export VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER=0 vllm serve ./NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --served-model-name nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --trust-remote-code --dtype bfloat16 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.94 \ --max-model-len 65536 --max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 192 \ --enable-chunked-prefill --no-enable-prefix-caching \ --use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none \ --mm-processor-cache-gb 0 --no-async-scheduling \ --limit-mm-per-prompt '{"audio":{"count":6,"length":120000000}}' \ --speculative-config '{"method":"mtp","num_speculative_tokens":8}' \ --reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 \ --trust-request-mm-kwargs \ --middleware nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm.ctc_serving.ctc_timestamp_middleware ``` The server listens on `127.0.0.1:8000`; use `--host` and `--port` to change this. The settings target an H100 with 80 GB of GPU memory; other hardware or workloads may need a different `--gpu-memory-utilization`, `--max-model-len`, or `--max-num-seqs`. The checkpoint contains two MTP depths implemented with a repeated layer. MTP8 reuses that layer to propose eight tokens; it does not require eight distinct trained MTP layers. The best mode depends on the GPU and the workload. These are rough throughput estimates, excluding server startup, for the English Open ASR and Monsoon datasets with reasoning disabled. Throughput depends on recording length, output length, batch size, and GPU memory settings; it is not a single-request latency estimate. Keep ReplaySSM (`--use-replayssm --mamba-backend flashinfer --mamba-cache-mode none`) and prefix caching disabled, as in the command above. The first requests after startup are slower while kernels are compiled and warmed up.
DFlash2 draft model As an alternative to MTP, the separate draft model [`nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2`](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2) proposes up to 15 tokens at once with vLLM's `dflash` method. DFlash2 and MTP are alternatives and are not combined. K=7 is the recommended starting point; K=15 was slower on the tested ASR workload. vLLM 0.32.0 needs a small fix to its DFlash2 implementation; without it, the server can fail when requests finish. Apply it once to the environment: ```bash python - <<'EOF_PATCH' from pathlib import Path import vllm path = Path(vllm.__file__).parent / "model_executor/models/qwen3_dflash2.py" source = path.read_text() if "safe_anchor_token_ids" not in source: old = " successors = successor_table[candidate_ids]\n" anchor = " anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k)," assert source.count(old) == 1 and source.count(anchor) == 1, "unexpected vLLM version" source = source.replace(old, ( " safe_anchor_token_ids = anchor_token_ids.clamp(\n" " min=0, max=predecessor_table.shape[0] - 1\n" " )\n" + old )).replace(anchor, " safe_anchor_token_ids[:, None, None].expand(-1, 1, top_k),") path.write_text(source) EOF_PATCH ``` The fix modifies vLLM source code (Copyright contributors to the vLLM project), which is licensed under the Apache License, Version 2.0, not under OpenMDW-1.1; see [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). Then start the server with the following options instead of `--speculative-config` and `--middleware` from the command above. Word timestamps are not available with DFlash2, so the CTC alignment is disabled: ```bash --speculative-config '{"method":"dflash","num_speculative_tokens":7,"model":"nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B-DFlash2"}' \ --hf-overrides '{"ctc_timestamps":{"enabled":false}}' ``` vLLM runs DFlash2 only on its V2 model runner, so also run `unset VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER` before starting the server.
#### Send a Request Send audio to the `/v1/chat/completions` endpoint with an OpenAI-compatible client. The following function covers transcription, reasoning, and word timestamps: ```python import base64 from pathlib import Path from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY") def ask(audio_path, prompt, system_prompt="", reasoning=False, timestamps=False): audio = base64.b64encode(Path(audio_path).read_bytes()).decode() messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system_prompt}] if system_prompt else [] messages.append({"role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio_url", "audio_url": {"url": f"data:audio/wav;base64,{audio}"}}, ]}) extra_body = { "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": reasoning}, "skip_special_tokens": False, # keep speaker and event tags "spaces_between_special_tokens": False, "seed": 0, } if reasoning: extra_body.update(top_k=-1, thinking_token_budget=17408) extra_body["chat_template_kwargs"]["reasoning_budget"] = 16384 if timestamps: extra_body["mm_processor_kwargs"] = {"capture_ctc_timestamps": True} return client.chat.completions.create( model="nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B", messages=messages, temperature=0.6 if reasoning else 0, top_p=0.95 if reasoning else 1.0, max_tokens=20480 if reasoning else 16384, extra_body=extra_body, ) response = ask("audio.wav", "Transcribe the following audio.") print(response.choices[0].message.content) ``` A dense one-hour conversation can need about 20,000 output tokens. For long recordings, raise `max_tokens` or remove it, so that the transcript is not truncated. Transcription uses temperature 0 with reasoning disabled. For audio understanding, enable reasoning and ask a question about the audio: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", "What is happening in this audio?", reasoning=True) ``` This sets temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k disabled, seed 0, a 20,480-token completion limit, and a 16,384-token reasoning budget with a 1,024-token allowance to finish reasoning. Use the task instructions documented under [Evaluation Prompts](#evaluation-prompts) as `prompt` and `system_prompt`. #### Word Timestamps and Speaker Diarization The checkpoint bundles the CTC heads used to align the generated transcript to the audio. With `--middleware` set as in the server command above, request timestamps with `timestamps=True`, together with a speaker-tagged transcription prompt: ```python response = ask("audio.wav", ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. " "Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. " "Write numbers in their standard written form. " "Put speaker tags on the transcription." ), timestamps=True) alignment = response.model_dump()["ctc_timestamps"] if alignment["error"] is not None: raise RuntimeError(alignment["error"]) for word in alignment["words"]: print(word["word"], word["start"], word["end"], word["speaker"]) ``` The response contains a top-level `ctc_timestamps` object: - `words`: word text, start and end times in seconds relative to the input audio, and the transcript's speaker tag. - `diarization`: speaker activity segments derived from the audio. - `speaker_tag_to_diarization_speaker`: the mapping between transcript tags and diarization speakers. - `error`: `null` on success, or an alignment failure reason. Check this field before using the timestamps. Timestamp requests accept one audio recording, `stream=false`, and `n=1`. Keep `skip_special_tokens=false` and ask for speaker tags when speaker attribution is needed. A transcript without speaker tags is aligned as a single speaker. Use the `diarization` segments, rather than word timestamps, when evaluating diarization. ### SGLang-Omni [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves this model for whole-file transcription on `/v1/audio/transcriptions`, on one GPU, from the BF16 or FP8 checkpoint (both validated on one H100 80 GB and one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). It does not need NeMo. After [installing SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md) 0.2.0, which pins SGLang 0.5.22: ```bash sgl-omni serve \ --model-path nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B \ --model-name nemotron-transcribe \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --port 8000 curl http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/transcriptions \ -F model=nemotron-transcribe \ -F file=@audio.wav ``` Word timestamps, speaker-attributed output, translation and speculative decoding are not part of this integration. See the [SGLang-Omni Nemotron Transcribe cookbook](https://sgl-project.github.io/sglang-omni/cookbook/nemotron_transcribe.html) for its settings, streaming and a tuned profile for short clips. ### Transformers usage 🤗 Install 🤗 Transformers from source: ```sh pip install git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers ```
Transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") audio = [samples + "en-Alice_woman.wav", samples + "diarization_example.mp3"] speaker_attributed_prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) prompt = [None, speaker_attributed_prompt] inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(audio, prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) texts = processor.decode(outputs[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print([text.replace(processor.tokenizer.pad_token, "") for text in texts]) ```
Speaker-attributed transcription ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) conversation = [ { "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "text", "text": prompt}, {"type": "audio", "path": samples + "diarization_example.mp3"}, ], } ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( conversation, tokenize=True, add_generation_prompt=True, return_dict=True, enable_thinking=False, ).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024) text = processor.decode(outputs[0, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) print(text) ``` `processor.extract_speaker_dict` splits the output into one dictionary per speaker turn: ```python for turn in processor.extract_speaker_dict(text): print(turn) ```
Word timestamps and speaker diarization Requires `torchaudio` and `scipy`. ```python from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoProcessor model_id = "nvidia/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe-30B-A4B" samples = "https://huggingface.co/datasets/hf-internal-testing/dummy-audio-samples/resolve/main/" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto") prompt = ( "Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write " "numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription." ) inputs = processor.apply_transcription_request(samples + "diarization_example.mp3", prompt=prompt).to(model.device) outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1024, return_word_timestamp_logits=True) texts = processor.decode(outputs.sequences[:, inputs.input_ids.shape[1] :], skip_special_tokens=False) timestamps = processor.align_word_timestamps( texts, outputs.word_timestamp_logits, inputs.input_features_mask, outputs.speaker_logits, ) print(timestamps[0]["chunks"][:3]) ```
See the [Transformers documentation](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/model_doc/nemotron3_5_transcribe) for more. ### Evaluation Prompts Use these shortened task-specific templates as starting points. For ASR evaluation, use [Exact ASR Benchmark Prompts](#exact-asr-benchmark-prompts). The ASR benchmark environment uses vLLM 0.28.0 and NeMo Speech with the FP32 preservation change from [PR #16357](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/pull/16357), which is included in the main branch, with MTP2. For audio understanding, spoken instructions, and text reasoning, use [Exact Understanding and Reasoning Prompts](#exact-understanding-and-reasoning-prompts), which lists the complete evaluated system prompts; keep the prepared user questions and choices unchanged. For the remaining benchmark families, use [All Evaluated Prompts](#all-evaluated-prompts), which contains the complete evaluated prompts and reasoning flags. Replace placeholders with the actual languages, labels, or context. #### Prompt Recommendations For these tasks, keep the **system prompt empty**. Send the instruction in the **user message**, alongside the audio. | Task | Recommended user prompt | Why we suggest it | | --- | --- | --- | | Verbatim ASR, including multilingual and long-form audio | `Audio transcription. Language: as spoken. Wording: verbatim, including fillers and repetitions. Formatting: punctuation and capitalization. Output: transcript only.` | Preserves wording and language with an explicit output format. | | Clean written transcript | Replace the wording clause above with `omit fillers and accidental repetitions; keep the remaining spoken wording unchanged`. Add `numbers in their standard written form` if needed. | Makes cleanup and number normalization explicit. | | Speaker attribution / word timestamps | `Transcribe this audio with punctuation and capitalization. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers in their standard written form. Put speaker tags on the transcription.` | Provides stable speaker tags for attribution and timestamp alignment; also enable timestamp capture. | | Near-field speaker only (experimental) | `Transcribe this audio. Include all spoken words and verbal fillers. Write numbers as spoken. No punctuation or capitalization. Transcribe only the speaker nearest to the microphone. Do not transcribe any other voices.` | Ignores background voices, such as far-field speech in a meeting room. With LibriSpeech test-clean speech mixed with far-field NOTSOFAR-1 audio, the WER is 4.78% with this prompt and 27.32% with a single-speaker transcription prompt. | | Code-switching / script control | `Transcribe verbatim in the original languages. Preserve hesitations and false starts. Write in

--- license: apache-2.0 language: - en - es - pt - de - fr - zh - ja - ru - ko pipeline_tag: audio-to-audio tags: - speech - full-duplex - speech-to-speech - haru --- # Haru-4B [Code](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru) · [Technical blog](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b/) · [Technical blog (Japanese)](https://blog.higurashi.ai/melte/haru4b-ja/) Haru-4B is a low-latency and multilingual full-duplex continuous spoken dialogue foundation model: it listens and speaks at the same time, the way people do on a phone call. It is a pretrained base model, released for research. - **Native full-duplex at 7.5 Hz.** Every 133 ms the model takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of its own audio and text. User audio, model audio and model text are summed into a single position of the language model, so listening and speaking never wait for each other. - **Continuous audio, one sampling step.** Audio is a 64-dimensional latent per frame. A small MLP head with MeanFlow sampling produces it in one step from the language model's hidden state; there is no separate audio transformer and there are no discrete audio tokens. - **Character and voice control.** A text card sets the character, a short reference clip sets the voice. - **Multilingual.** English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Korean.

## Usage The code is at : a PyTorch implementation with a web demo, an MLX implementation with a native macOS app, and a plugin for serving with vLLM-Omni. With an NVIDIA GPU (about 12 GB of memory): ```bash git clone https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru && cd Haru pip install -e ./haru python -m haru.server --hf-repo higurashi-ai/Haru-4B ``` Open , pick a character, give the model a voice, and talk. For low latency, we recommend wired headphones and a wired microphone. Bluetooth devices add 100 ms or more. **Bring your own voice.** Haru ships without voice clips. Upload or record a clip of the voice the model should speak with: one speaker, 3 seconds to 3 minutes, clean speech. Only use voices you have the right to use. ```python from haru import DuplexSession, HaruModel from haru.audio import load_audio, prepare_reference model = HaruModel.from_pretrained("higurashi-ai/Haru-4B") voice = prepare_reference(load_audio("voice.wav")) session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice) frame = session.start() # the model's first 133 ms: frame.audio, frame.text while not frame.done: frame = session.step(user_audio) # 3200 samples at 24 kHz in, 3200 out ``` The system prompt is a character card with a fixed layout; the repository's README shows how to build one. ## Files | File | Contents | | --- | --- | | `model.safetensors` | All weights (bfloat16): `lm.*` language model, `model_audio_proj.*` / `user_audio_proj.*` audio input projections, `head.*` MeanFlow head, `codec.*` audio codec | | `config.json` | Model configuration | | `tokenizer.json` | Text tokenizer | ## Architecture | Part | Details | | --- | --- | | Language model | Qwen3.5-4B text backbone, 32 layers, hidden size 2560 | | Audio codec | VibeVoice acoustic tokenizer, causal, 24 kHz, 3200 samples per latent | | Audio head | 4-layer MLP, MeanFlow, 1 sampling step, guidance scale 1 to 2 (default 1.5) | | Frame rate | 7.5 Hz | ## Limitations Haru-4B is a pretrained base model, released for research. It holds a natural conversation, but it is not a reliable source of facts and does not follow instructions the way an assistant does. It can imitate the voice of a reference clip; only use voices you have the right to use. ## License The weights are released under the Apache License 2.0.

# Haru-4B GGUF (ROCmFPX)

GGUF files of [higurashi-ai/Haru-4B](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B), a full-duplex spoken dialogue
model by higurashi-ai, with a native C++ runtime (`llama-haru`) in the
[ROCmFPX fork of llama.cpp](https://github.com/HarshaVardhan3002/ROCmFPX).

Haru listens and speaks at the same time. Every 133 ms it takes one frame of your audio and produces one frame of
its own audio and text. The language model is a Qwen3.5-4B text backbone. A small MeanFlow head turns its hidden
state into a 64-dim audio latent, and a causal VibeVoice codec turns that into 24 kHz audio. All credit for the
model goes to higurashi-ai (and to the Qwen team for the backbone). See the
[original card](https://huggingface.co/higurashi-ai/Haru-4B) and the [Haru code](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru).

## Files

| File | Size | What it is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Haru-4B-Q8_0_ROCMFPX.gguf` | 4.37 GB | Language model, ROCmFPX 8-bit with tensor scales (needs the fork). Recommended |
| `Haru-4B-Q8_0.gguf` | 4.48 GB | Language model, stock Q8_0 (runs on any llama.cpp build) |
| `Haru-4B-Q6_0_ROCMFPX.gguf` | 3.48 GB | Language model, ROCmFPX 6-bit with tensor scales (needs the fork) |
| `Haru-4B-audio-F16.gguf` | 2.30 GB | Audio parts: the two audio projectors, the MeanFlow head and the codec (needed with either model) |

You need one language model file and the audio file.

## Run it

Build the fork, then run an offline conversation from two WAV files (24 kHz mono):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/HarshaVardhan3002/ROCmFPX && cd ROCmFPX
cmake -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release && cmake --build build --target llama-haru -j

./build/bin/llama-haru -m Haru-4B-Q8_0_ROCMFPX.gguf --audio Haru-4B-audio-F16.gguf \
    --voice my_voice.wav --user question.wav --card-file card.txt -o answer.wav
```

- `--voice`: the voice Haru speaks with. One speaker, 3 seconds to 3 minutes, clean speech.
- `--user`: what you say. Haru listens to it frame by frame and answers while it plays.
- `--card` / `--card-file`: the character card (system prompt). The
  [Haru README](https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru) shows the card layout the model was trained with.
- Output: `answer.wav` (Haru's channel) and `answer-stereo.wav` (you on the left, Haru on the right).
  Haru's text appears on the terminal as it speaks.
- Sampling defaults follow the official code: temperature 0.7, top-k 25, guidance 1.5, DRY on.
  `--speak-first`, `--seed`, `--temp`, `--guidance` and `--tail` (seconds of listening after your clip) are available.

The runtime is an offline (file in, file out) tool for now. A live microphone mode is not part of this release.

## Accuracy

The runtime was checked part by part against the official PyTorch code in float32, on a real voice clip and
24 live dialogue frames:

| Part | Cosine similarity to PyTorch |
| --- | --- |
| Codec encode (whole clip and streaming), streaming decode | 1.000000 |
| Audio projectors (input embeddings) | 1.000000 |
| Language model hidden states | 0.999998 |
| Text logits | 0.999999 (same top token on 24 / 24 frames) |
| MeanFlow head latents | 1.000000 |

Quantized language models, KL divergence to BF16 on wiki text (40 x 512 tokens), and hidden-state similarity on the
real dialogue frames (file run as is on the CPU):

| Language model | Size | Wiki KLD | Dialogue hidden cosine |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Q8_0_ROCMFPX (this repo) | 4.37 GB | 0.0019 | 0.9966 |
| Q8_0 (this repo) | 4.48 GB | 0.0031 | 0.9954 |
| Q6_0_ROCMFPX (this repo) | 3.48 GB | 0.0113 | 0.9915 |
| stock Q6_K (not uploaded) | 3.46 GB | 0.0153 | 0.9913 |

On the CPU, use the fork at commit `4310e2480` or newer for the ROCmFPX 8-bit file. Older builds rounded the
activations to 8 bits before each matrix multiply, which brought this file down to 0.966 on the dialogue frames.
The audio file in F16 matches the float32 one (head cosine 0.9999997).

## Notes and limits

- Verified on the CPU (ARM). On a CPU it is slower than real time; real-time use needs a GPU build. GPU backends
  have not been tested with this runtime yet.
- Haru-4B is a pretrained base model released for research. It holds a natural conversation, but it is not a
  reliable source of facts and does not follow instructions the way an assistant does.
- It can imitate the voice of a reference clip. Only use voices you have the right to use.

Apache License 2.0, same as the original weights.

# Stable Audio 3 Small SFX · Calibrated DiT GGUF

DiT and the original conditioner for local sound-effect generation. Powered by Stability AI.

**Русский.** Диффузионная модель DiT и кондиционер для локальной генерации звуковых эффектов. Для запуска на CPU нужны совместимые SAME-S и T5Gemma.

## Evidence / Проверка

Recorded projection error **9,307 → 8,950**. Calibration used Vulkan and the local sa3.cpp pipeline uses the CPU for inference.

Projection error measures calibration fit on the recorded workload. Ошибка проекций характеризует подгонку на записанной выборке.

[Calibration runs / Замеры калибровки](https://github.com/aktalascloud/gguf-converter/blob/v1.9.0/benchmarks/2026-11-17-whole-gsq-rco-rx580.json)

## Files / Файлы

- [stable-audio-3-small-sfx-conditioner-v1.0-F32.gguf](./stable-audio-3-small-sfx-conditioner-v1.0-F32.gguf) · 793,184 bytes
- [stable-audio-3-small-sfx-dit-0.5B-v1.0-Q8_0-Q6_K-GSQ-RCO-Vulkan-2026-11-17.gguf](./stable-audio-3-small-sfx-dit-0.5B-v1.0-Q8_0-Q6_K-GSQ-RCO-Vulkan-2026-11-17.gguf) · 489,208,512 bytes

**Companions / Компоненты**  
[Stable-Audio-3-Small-SFX-SAME-S-GSQ-RCO-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/TalasCloud/Stable-Audio-3-Small-SFX-SAME-S-GSQ-RCO-GGUF) · [T5Gemma-B-B-UL2-F16-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/TalasCloud/T5Gemma-B-B-UL2-F16-GGUF)

## Sources

- [Stability AI / original model and terms](https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-audio-3-small-sfx)
- [thepatch / input GGUF conversion](https://huggingface.co/thepatch/stable-audio-3-small-sfx-GGUF/tree/fcbd756cde8f9cc4d0213433d868063593d6ca22)

## Weights and hardware

Format: **Q8_0, Q6_K**.
Tensor layout: Q8_0 × 152, Q6_K × 20, F32 × 245, F16 × 20.
